title: The Professional: A conversation with Professor Wilkins
author: David B. Wilkins

dom.t: Lawyer development: AI renews lifelong competence reform

st.t: Career inequality: Professional change preserves unequal rewards
st.an: The source treats restructuring as a premise for investigation and advocates systematic career information, but it offers no findings on whether professional change preserves hierarchies or whether prestige and social background continue to shape rewards. It aligns with the cluster’s research and guidance agenda without establishing a position on its central inequality claim.
qs: What are the central questions the program wants to crack?**  It starts from the premise that we are in the midst of a kind of global restructuring of legal and professional services, and we want to understand why it’s happened, how it’s happened, and what its implications are for the legal profession.

It’s also the law school’s obligation to those lawyers after they graduate to provide them with unbiased and systematic information on the large questions that are affecting their professional careers and the world in which they live and compete.

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk
st.an: Wilkins treats global restructuring of legal services as a premise for research and assigns law schools responsibility for studying and explaining professional change. This broadly fits the cluster’s institutional-adaptation theme, but the source predates and does not address AI, junior-pipeline risk, productivity, or lawyer displacement, so it cannot establish a position on the cluster’s principal proposition.

st.t: Lawyer development: AI renews lifelong competence reform
st.an: Wilkins supports the cluster’s core case that legal education must extend beyond individual legal analysis to prepare lawyers for institutional practice and broader public responsibilities. The source does not address AI readiness, verification or the funding of lifelong apprenticeship directly, so its support is concentrated on integrated professional preparation and public purpose.
qs: If you look at a state prosecutor’s office, a general counsel’s office, the size of a legal services office or a legal clinic, law is increasingly an institutionalized profession, and we teach our students very little about practicing law in an institutional context.
Law schools have an obligation to train lawyers in a way that serves the broader public purposes that lawyers have the privilege to serve.

kp.k: Global restructuring motivates research into professional and public consequences
kp.d: In this 2005 interview, David Wilkins describes global restructuring of legal and professional services as the premise of his research program, rather than a demonstrated research finding. He calls for investigation of its causes, processes and consequences for lawyers and wider political, economic and social life. The interview discusses organizational change and technology generally, not AI.
qs: It starts from the premise that we are in the midst of a kind of global restructuring of legal and professional services, and we want to understand why it’s happened, how it’s happened, and what its implications are for the legal profession.

kp.k: Law schools owe research and training obligations beyond graduation
kp.d: Wilkins argues that law schools should provide graduates with unbiased, systematic information about changes affecting their careers. He also grounds an obligation to consumers of legal services in the profession's licensing privileges, arguing that training must serve broader public purposes.
qs: It’s also the law school’s obligation to those lawyers after they graduate to provide them with unbiased and systematic information on the large questions that are affecting their professional careers and the world in which they live and compete.
Law schools have an obligation to train lawyers in a way that serves the broader public purposes that lawyers have the privilege to serve.

kp.k: Individual-focused education neglects increasingly institutional legal practice
kp.d: Wilkins identifies the largest educational gap as a focus on individual practice and decision-making despite increasingly large, bureaucratic practice organizations. He extends this diagnosis beyond private firms to prosecutors, general counsel offices, legal services offices and clinics. As a historical illustration, he states that the world's largest firm had about 160 lawyers in 1965; he supplies no underlying study.
qs: The biggest gap stems from the fact that we focus almost entirely on law as an individual practice about individual decision making. But law is increasingly practiced in organizations and institutions of increasingly large and bureaucratic size.
In 1965, the largest law firm in the world had about 160 lawyers.
law is increasingly an institutionalized profession, and we teach our students very little about practicing law in an institutional context.

kp.k: Consolidation does not establish a single winning organizational model
kp.d: Asked whether specialization or expansion and mergers will prevail, Wilkins says the outcome remains unknown. He distinguishes earlier predictions that law firms would rapidly reach major accounting firms' size from his assertion that many mergers fail to deliver expected efficiency gains. He sees consolidation occurring alongside a proliferation of practice settings.
qs: Well, I think we don’t know yet.
A few years ago it was popular to talk about consolidation and to hypothesize that we would very quickly get to the point where law firms were the size of the major accounting firms.
Now we know that many law firm mergers, just like many mergers in general, fail to produce the efficiency gains that the people thought they would.
I think we’re seeing consolidation, but we’re also seeing the proliferation of practice settings.

kp.k: Distance-spanning technology enables experimentation with alternative practice models
kp.d: Wilkins argues that technology permits geographically dispersed lawyers and other professionals to collaborate on international projects. His New Hampshire–Beijing–Singapore–Rio de Janeiro example illustrates a possibility, not a documented case or the norm. He predicts greater organizational variety as working across distance becomes easier.
qs: And technology is pushing this, because now you can be sitting in your cabin in New Hampshire and be linked up instantaneously with lawyers in Beijing and investment bankers in Singapore about a project in Rio de Janeiro.
Of course, that’s not the norm, but people are experimenting with it, and the more technology allows people to work easily across distance, the more you’re going to see different models developing.

kp.k: High turnover drives recruitment, requiring active career self-management
kp.d: Wilkins advises students entering large firms to monitor their careers rather than assume employers will protect their interests. He reports annual turnover of 'something like 20 to 25 percent in many law firms' as a reason firms recruit large numbers. This is an approximate contemporary assertion without a stated sample or methodology, not an AI displacement claim.
qs: But my most important advice is to keep your eyes open and to pay careful attention to what’s happening to your career because nobody really is looking out for you.
Turnover is reaching something like 20 to 25 percent in many law firms, per year. In order to keep the enterprise going, they have to hire very large numbers of people.

kp.k: Challenging assignments underpin skill formation and career success
kp.d: Wilkins identifies access to appropriate work, especially challenging 'stretch' assignments, as a determinant of success within firms. His mechanism links assignments to developing higher-order skills and demonstrating competence to others.
qs: How well you do in a law firm depends on what kind of work you get and whether you get what they call in the business school world “stretch” assignments—assignments that challenge you, give you the opportunity to develop higher-order skills and show other people that you know your stuff.

kp.k: Broader careers and technology may revive smaller practices
kp.d: Wilkins balances career risks with his view that law is more meritocratic and open than previously and that legal training supports a wider range of rewarding careers. He names investment banking, consulting, major accounting firms and technology companies as destinations. He separately predicts a renaissance of solo and small-firm practice because technology expands what practitioners can accomplish with their human capital; this is a forecast, not evidence of an observed revival.
qs: Law, in many ways, is much more of a meritocracy and is more open today than it ever has been before.
A huge number of people now go into investment banking or consulting or work in a major accounting firm or a technology company.
I think we’re going to see a renaissance of solo and small-firm practice, because technology allows people to leverage their human capital in ways that were simply impossible before.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The source makes no AI-specific claims. Interviewee David B. Wilkins attributes diversification of legal practice models and a predicted revival of solo and small-firm practice to technology generally.
pts.d: Wilkins claims that technology enables geographically dispersed collaboration and encourages new practice settings alongside law-firm consolidation. He predicts a renaissance of solo and small-firm practice because technology enables practitioners to make greater use of their human capital. These are general technology claims in a 2005 interview, not claims about AI, automation or lawyer substitution. His reference to leveraging human capital does not describe associate-to-partner staffing leverage.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Wilkins offers qualitative professional observations and an illustrative collaboration scenario, not empirical evidence measuring technology’s effects.
pts.d: The geographically dispersed project illustrates a capability rather than a documented case. Wilkins says people are experimenting with such arrangements, but supplies no named examples, study, dataset or quantified outcome supporting either technology-related claim. The interview identifies him as director of HLS’s Program on the Legal Profession and its affiliated research center; the claims are presented as his assessment.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern developments underway in November 2005 and an unspecified future, conditional on technology making remote collaboration easier.
pts.d: Wilkins describes remote collaboration and experimentation as already possible at the time of the interview, while expressly qualifying them as not the norm. He expects more practice models as working across distance becomes easier. His solo and small-firm renaissance prediction has no deadline. He does not declare either consolidation or specialization the eventual winning model.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The technology claims concern geographically dispersed practitioners, solo and small firms, and students considering legal careers.
pts.d: Lawyers and other professionals are portrayed as able to collaborate internationally without co-location. Solo and small-firm practitioners are expected to gain opportunities through technology-enabled use of their human capital. Wilkins frames this as an encouraging career prospect for students. He does not specify AI-related effects on staffing, fees, clients or access to justice.
